--- Slide/Halaman 24 ---
Organization of Genes

Genetic information in bacteria is stored as a 
sequence of DNA bases
•
The orientation of the two DNA strands 
is antiparallel
•
Template strand & coding strand

Bacteriophages and virusesDNA or RNA 
•
RNA most frequently occurs in single-
stranded form
24


--- Slide/Halaman 25 ---
Prokaryotic Genome

Most prokaryotic genomes (>90%) consist of a single circular DNA 
molecule
‐
Two circular DNA molecules: Brucella melitensis, Burkholderia
pseudomallei, and Vibrio cholerae

Bacterial genes are haploid

Pathogenicity islands 
‐
Specific cluster genes encoded virulence factors
‐
Different G + C content
‐
Closely linked on the chromosome to tRNA genes
‐
Flanked by direct repeats
‐
Contain diverse genes important for pathogenesis
‐
antibiotic resistance, adhesins, invasins, and exotoxins
25


--- Slide/Halaman 26 ---
Viral Genome

Replication of the viral genome depends on the metabolic energy 
and the macromolecular synthetic machinery of the host
‐
genetic information required for replication of the viral 
components, packaging and liberating the resulting virus from 
the host cell.

The nucleic acid molecule of bacteriophages (phage) is 
‐
surrounded by a protein coat
‐
contain double-stranded DNA;                                                                        
others contain double-stranded RNA

Many phages contain specialized syringe-like structure                                         
(tails) that bind to receptors on the cell surface and                                                
inject the phage nucleic acid into a host cell
26

Feto-Maternal Transmission
‐
Virus from the maternal circulation infects cells of the 
placenta fetal circulation all tissues of the 
developing fetus
‐
During birth when the fetus comes into contact with 
infected genital secretions of the mother
‐
After birth when the infant ingests infected breast milk
‐
Fetal death or developmental abnormalities

Waterborne Disease
53
Waterborne pathogens include bacteria, viruses, and parasitic protists.
Drinking or food preparation or from water used for swimming and bathing

Potable water filtration and chlorination.
A widely used indicator for microbial water contamination is the coliform group of 
bacteria inhabit the intestinal tract of humans and other animals Escherichia 
coli

Diagnosis Mycrobiology
59
Clinical microbiology laboratory 
Identifying the organism causing an infectious disease
important in diagnosis and control of infectious disease
•Determine the antimicrobial activity
•Initial Treatment Definitive microbiologic diagnosis


--- Slide/Halaman 60 ---
1. Direct microscopic visualization of the organism
2. Cultivation and identification of the organism
3. Detection of microbial antigens and antibodies serologic diagnosis
4. Detection of microbial DNA or RNA
5. Detection of an inflammatory or host immune response to the 
microorganism
Diagnosis Mycrobiology


--- Slide/Halaman 61 ---
Direct microscopic visualization of 
the organism
61
Directly visualized by microscopic examination of patient specimens
Morphology and staining characteristics
Gram staining: Gram negative & Gram positive differ in their susceptibility to various 
antibiotic
Limitations: The number of microorganisms required is relatively 
high
Example: gram-negative intracellular diplococci in urethral pus 
provide a presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea


--- Slide/Halaman 62 ---
Cultivation and Identification of The 
Organism
62
Identified using such characteristics as colony size, shape, color, hemolytic reactions on 
solid media, odor, and metabolic properties
Success of culturing depends on appropriate collection and transport
techniques and on selection of appropriate culture media
Speciment collection: transport media must be used to
extend the viability of the organism to be cultured
Most bacteria require varying numbers of growth factors: organic 
compound
Oxygen requirement


--- Slide/Halaman 63 ---
Detection of Microbial Antigens
63
Determining metabolic properties of the unknown bacterium
Enzyme tests: catalase test, oxidase test, urease, coagulase etc.
Immunologic system: detection of microbial antigen with known antiserum
Quellung reaction: unkown bacteria + identifies specific antibodies capsule “swell” 
S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis groups A and C


--- Slide/Halaman 64 ---
Detection of Microbial Antibodies
64
Detection in a patient’s serum of antibodies that are directed against microbial antigens 
provides evidence for a current or past infection with a specific pathogen
Antibody may not be detectable early in an infection
Techniques: complement fixation, agglutination, ELISA
Direct agglutination: measures the ability of a 
patient's serum antibody to directly agglutinate 
specific killed microorganisms
Immunoassays for cell-associated antigen 
(immunohistology)


--- Slide/Halaman 65 ---
Detection of Microbial DNA or RNA
65
Techniques: 
1. direct hybridization
2. amplification methods using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
3. DNA microarrays
Single-stranded probe DNA (or RNA) is used to detect complementary RNA or 
denatured DNA in a test specimen
The nucleic acid probe typically is labeled with enzymes, antigenic substrates, 
chemiluminescent molecules, or radioisotopes to facilitate detection of the hybridization 
product
